Hook

Top hooks, yt-script score

  • 0In 1919 Germany signed a treaty that made the next world war almost certain.
  • 0In June 1940, Hitler took France in six weeks. It started with a promise on a piece of paper.

Look and device

Running device

One big parchment map of Europe that the story keeps returning to. Germany is a grey blob with a frowning face; every country it swallows turns grey, and a running counter in the corner ticks up the countries taken. A ticking 'deal clock' marks every broken promise.

Look

Map-driven history explainer in the house 2D style, Leo sheet character style (as in Ancient Humans and Rothschilds). Painted plates: a Versailles hall of mirrors, a 1923 Berlin bakery queue with wheelbarrows of cash, a Munich conference table, a Polish plain with horses and tanks, a dark Ardennes forest road, the beach at Dunkirk with little boats, a London radio studio. Muted parchment, navy and brick red; German forces in plain grey with no insignia. SFX under the VO (radio crackle, marching, tank rumble, aircraft, waves), music only at combine.

Act 1: The Treaty Everyone Hated

0:37 · 5 shots · 88 words
  1. 1.01WIDE7.5s

    1919. World War One is over, and the winners meet at Versailles, near Paris, to write the peace.

    A grand hall of mirrors; leaders around a long table.

    VERSAILLES · 1919

    ANIMATIONChandeliers glint; pens scratch.

  2. 1.02CU8.3s

    One line, Article 231, put the blame for the war's losses on Germany. Germans called it the war guilt clause.

    A treaty page; Article 231 circled in red.

    ARTICLE 231

    ANIMATIONRed circle draws itself.

  3. 1.03MED10.2s

    France and Britain wanted Germany to pay. In 1921 the bill was set at 132 billion gold marks, about 33 billion dollars at the time.

    A giant invoice unrolling across the floor toward a small grey Germany.

    132 BILLION GOLD MARKS

    ANIMATIONInvoice keeps unrolling.

  4. 1.04CU5.3s

    Germany didn't finish paying off the last of those debts until 2010.

    A calendar flipping from 1921 to 2010.

    FINAL PAYMENT: 2010

    ANIMATIONPages flip fast.

  5. 1.05MED5.7s

    The army was cut to 100,000 men. No air force. Almost no navy.

    A tiny row of soldiers; crossed-out planes and ships.

    100,000 MEN · NO AIR FORCE

    ANIMATIONRed X stamps on a plane and a ship.

Act 2: Bread for 200 Billion Marks

0:39 · 5 shots · 94 words
  1. 2.01MED5.7s

    To pay, Germany printed money. By 1923 prices were doubling every few days.

    A printing press spitting out banknotes.

    ANIMATIONNotes fly out of the press.

  2. 2.02CU8.3s

    In Berlin, a loaf of bread cost about 160 marks in 1922. By November 1923 it cost around 200 billion.

    A bakery counter; the price tag spins upward.

    160 → 200,000,000,000

    ANIMATIONPrice tag digits blur upward.

  3. 2.03MED5.7s

    People carried cash in wheelbarrows. Savings built over a lifetime were worth nothing.

    A man pushing a wheelbarrow full of notes to buy one loaf.

    ANIMATIONWheelbarrow wobbles; notes blow away.

  4. 2.04MED12.1s

    In this chaos, a young agitator named Adolf Hitler tried to seize power in Munich in 1923. The coup failed and he went to prison, but it made him famous.

    A beer hall; a silhouetted speaker on a chair; then prison bars.

    MUNICH · 1923

    ANIMATIONSilhouette only; bars slide across.

  5. 2.05MED7.5s

    He blamed Germany's humiliation on Jews and on communists. It was a lie, but angry, frightened people listened.

    Propaganda posters going up on a wall, blurred and stamped FALSE.

    A LIE

    ANIMATIONFALSE stamp slams on the posters.

Act 3: Breaking the Rules

0:46 · 6 shots · 111 words
  1. 3.01MED7.5s

    Then came the Great Depression in 1929. By early 1933 about six million Germans were out of work.

    A long queue outside a closed factory.

    6,000,000 UNEMPLOYED

    ANIMATIONQueue shuffles; a gate stays shut.

  2. 3.02MED7.5s

    In January 1933 Hitler became chancellor. Within months he had banned other parties and made himself a dictator.

    A silhouette at a podium; party office doors slammed and padlocked.

    1933

    ANIMATIONPadlocks click shut one by one.

  3. 3.03MED7.2s

    His plan was an empire for a so-called master race, with 'living space' taken from the east.

    The map: arrows pointing east from Germany.

    'LIVING SPACE'

    ANIMATIONArrows stretch east.

  4. 3.04MED9.8s

    In 1935 he revealed an air force and brought back conscription, breaking the treaty. Britain even signed a deal letting Germany build a navy.

    Planes roll out of a hangar; a British signature on a naval deal.

    TREATY BROKEN

    ANIMATIONHangar doors open; pen signs.

  5. 3.05CU6.8s

    In 1936 his troops marched into the Rhineland, next to France. France and Britain did nothing.

    Grey soldiers crossing a bridge; French and British leaders shrugging.

    RHINELAND · 1936

    ANIMATIONBoots thud; a shrug.

  6. 3.06MED7.5s

    France was already relying on the Maginot Line, a huge chain of forts along its border with Germany.

    A long concrete fortress wall with guns pointing east.

    MAGINOT LINE

    ANIMATIONCamera pans along the wall.

Act 4: Austria and the Paper Peace

0:52 · 6 shots · 127 words
  1. 4.01MED7.5s

    In February 1938 Hitler summoned Austria's chancellor, Kurt Schuschnigg, and bullied him into putting Nazis in his government.

    Two men at a desk; one looming silhouette, one small chancellor.

    FEB 1938

    ANIMATIONSilhouette looms larger.

  2. 4.02MED10.2s

    Schuschnigg called a vote on independence. Before it could happen, German troops crossed the border. On 13 March 1938 Austria was declared part of Germany.

    A ballot box; then grey troops marching into Vienna; the map turns Austria grey.

    AUSTRIA · 13 MARCH 1938

    ANIMATIONBallot box tips over; map flips grey. Counter 1.

  3. 4.03MED7.9s

    Next was the Sudetenland, a border region of Czechoslovakia where about three million German speakers lived. Hitler demanded it.

    The map zooms to Czechoslovakia; its edge glows.

    SUDETENLAND

    ANIMATIONBorder region pulses.

  4. 4.04WIDE9.1s

    In September 1938 Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, met Hitler in Munich with France and Italy. Czechoslovakia wasn't even in the room.

    A conference table in Munich; an empty chair labelled CZECHOSLOVAKIA.

    MUNICH · SEPT 1938

    ANIMATIONSpotlight on the empty chair.

  5. 4.05CU10.6s

    They handed him the Sudetenland in return for a promise of no more war. Chamberlain flew home waving the paper and promised 'peace for our time'.

    Chamberlain with an umbrella waving a paper at an airfield; the deal clock starts ticking.

    'PEACE FOR OUR TIME'

    ANIMATIONPaper flutters; clock ticks.

  6. 4.06MED7.2s

    Six months later, in March 1939, German troops took the rest of Czechoslovakia. The promise was worthless.

    The paper tears in half; the map turns Czechoslovakia grey.

    MARCH 1939

    ANIMATIONPaper rips; map flips grey. Counter 2.

Act 5: Poland and the Lightning War

0:59 · 7 shots · 142 words
  1. 5.01MED10.2s

    Poland was next. To make it safe, Hitler did something shocking: in August 1939 he signed a pact with his sworn enemy, Stalin's Soviet Union.

    Two silhouettes shaking hands over a map; a hidden page with a line through Poland.

    NAZI-SOVIET PACT · AUG 1939

    ANIMATIONHandshake; a secret page slides out.

  2. 5.02CU3.8s

    Secretly they agreed to split Poland between them.

    A pencil line drawn down the middle of Poland.

    SECRET DEAL

    ANIMATIONPencil cuts the map.

  3. 5.03WIDE8.3s

    On 1 September 1939, about one and a half million German troops invaded Poland from the west, north and south.

    Grey arrows plunge into Poland from three sides.

    1 SEPTEMBER 1939

    ANIMATIONArrows punch in; rumble.

  4. 5.04MED7.9s

    Two days later Britain and France declared war on Germany. Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada soon followed.

    A radio crackling; flags of the Allies popping up.

    3 SEPTEMBER 1939

    ANIMATIONRadio crackle; flags pop.

  5. 5.05MED11.3s

    Germany used a new way of fighting: tanks smashing through fast, planes bombing from above, no time for the enemy to react. It was called Blitzkrieg, lightning war.

    Tanks racing across a plain with dive bombers overhead; a lightning bolt.

    BLITZKRIEG = LIGHTNING WAR

    ANIMATIONTanks rush; lightning cracks.

  6. 5.06CU7.2s

    Many German soldiers were given Pervitin, a methamphetamine pill, to keep them awake and fighting for days.

    A small tin of pills labelled PERVITIN; a soldier's wide-open eyes.

    PERVITIN = METH

    ANIMATIONPill tin pops open.

  7. 5.07MED10.2s

    Poland's army still relied heavily on horses. On 17 September the Soviets invaded from the east. By early October, Poland was gone, split in two.

    Horses facing tanks on a plain; then the map splits Poland grey and red.

    POLAND · OCT 1939

    ANIMATIONMap halves fill. Counter 3.

Act 6: The Phony War and the Fall of Norway

0:49 · 5 shots · 120 words
  1. 6.01MED10.6s

    Then, strangely, almost nothing happened in the west. Britain and France had declared war, but for months they barely fought. People called it the Phony War.

    French soldiers playing cards behind the Maginot Line; a yawning sentry.

    THE PHONY WAR

    ANIMATIONCards slap; sentry yawns.

  2. 6.02MED9.1s

    Stalin, meanwhile, attacked Finland in November 1939. Leningrad was only about 30 kilometres from the Finnish border, and he wanted a buffer.

    Snowy forest; Finnish ski troops in white.

    WINTER WAR

    ANIMATIONSnow falls; skis swish.

  3. 6.03CU10.6s

    Finland on the map loses a slice in the east.

    FINLAND KEPT ITS FREEDOM

    ANIMATIONSlice peels off; Finland's face stays defiant.

  4. 6.04MED10.2s

    On 9 April 1940 Germany struck Denmark and Norway. Denmark fell in hours; Norway fought for two months. Its king and government escaped to London.

    Grey arrows into Denmark and Norway; a ship sailing to London.

    9 APRIL 1940

    ANIMATIONArrows; ship sails west. Counter 5.

  5. 6.05MED8.7s

    In Britain, Chamberlain's policy of giving in had failed. On 10 May 1940 he resigned, and Winston Churchill became prime minister.

    Chamberlain leaving 10 Downing Street; Churchill with a cigar arriving.

    CHURCHILL · 10 MAY 1940

Act 7: Through the Forest Nobody Watched

1:09 · 8 shots · 167 words
  1. 7.01WIDE9.1s

    That same day, Germany attacked the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and France, with around three million soldiers and thousands of tanks and planes.

    The map: three grey arrow groups labelled A, B and C.

    10 MAY 1940

    ANIMATIONArrows labelled A, B, C appear.

  2. 7.02MED9.4s

    Group B swept into the Netherlands and Belgium, drawing the best British and French troops north. Group C sat facing the Maginot Line.

    Allied troops rushing north on the map; grey troops staring at the wall.

    ANIMATIONAllied arrows race north into the trap.

  3. 7.03MED9.4s

    THE ARDENNES

    ANIMATIONHeadlights in the trees; engines rumble.

  4. 7.04CU9.1s

    They broke through at Sedan on 13 May and raced to the sea. The Allied armies in the north were cut off.

    A grey arrow slices across France to the coast.

    SEDAN · 13 MAY

    ANIMATIONThe arrow cuts the map in two.

  5. 7.05WIDE7.5s

    Hundreds of thousands of soldiers were trapped on the beaches at Dunkirk with the sea at their backs.

    A long beach crowded with soldiers; smoke over the town.

    DUNKIRK

    ANIMATIONWaves; distant planes.

  6. 7.06MED8.7s

    Little boats crossing the Channel; Spitfire-style planes above.

    OPERATION DYNAMO

Fact log

Fixes against the transcript

  • Reparations: London Schedule 1921, 132 billion gold marks (about $33 billion then); final bond interest payment 3 Oct 2010.
  • Bread prices: Berlin, about 163 marks (1922) to about 200 billion marks (Nov 1923).
  • Hitler appointed chancellor 30 Jan 1933; dictatorship via Enabling Act (Mar 1933) and one-party state (Jul 1933). Transcript's 'declared himself dictator' corrected.
  • Luftwaffe revealed and conscription restored March 1935; Anglo-German Naval Agreement June 1935; Rhineland remilitarised March 1936 (added).
  • Maginot Line built from 1929, before Hitler took power; transcript implied it was a response to him. Length figure dropped.
  • Anschluss: troops crossed 12 Mar 1938, Austria annexed 13 Mar; Schuschnigg resigned 11 Mar. Transcript's Fischböck detail dropped.
  • Munich Agreement 30 Sep 1938 (Germany, Britain, France, Italy; Czechoslovakia excluded).
  • Poland: invaded 1 Sep 1939 with about 1.5 million troops (transcript said 1 million); Soviets invaded 17 Sep; last resistance ended 6 Oct. Transcript's 'occupied 8 Sept / under a week' corrected.
  • Polish cavalry charging tanks is a myth; script says only that the army relied heavily on horses.
  • Winter War 30 Nov 1939 to 13 Mar 1940 (over 3 months); Leningrad about 32 km from the border (transcript said 50 km); Finland ceded about 11% of territory.
  • Norway campaign 9 Apr to 10 Jun 1940; Denmark fell in hours.
  • Dunkirk: Operation Dynamo 26 May to 4 Jun 1940, about 338,000 evacuated (transcript said 350,000).
  • Pact of Steel signed May 1939; Italy declared war 10 Jun 1940; French armistice 22 Jun 1940.
  • Churchill's 'fight on the beaches' speech 4 Jun 1940 (paraphrased, not quoted at length).

Removed from the transcript

  • Source creator's catchphrases, video plugs and Part 2 tease removed; everything rewritten in our own words.
  • Hitler's rise kept to a few lines (no detail on propaganda campaigns).
  • Nolan's Dunkirk film reference cut.
  • Real dictators (Hitler, Stalin, Mussolini) shown only as silhouettes; no swastikas; antisemitic posters blurred and stamped FALSE.
